items.text: Obtaining large-scale annotated data for NLP tasks in the scientiﬁc domain is challenging and expensive.
items.why: States the main problem driving the research.
items.plain: Getting large annotated datasets for language processing tasks in science is hard and costly.

items.text: We release SCIBERT, a pretrained language model based on BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) to address the lack of high-quality, large-scale labeled scientiﬁc data.
items.why: Introduces the main solution released by the paper.
items.plain: We release SCIBERT, a pretrained language model based on BERT, to help with the lack of large labeled scientific datasets.

items.text: We demonstrate statistically signiﬁcant improvements over BERT and achieve new state-of-theart results on several of these tasks.
items.why: Summarizes overall performance gains over baseline.
items.plain: We show statistically significant improvements over BERT and reach new top results on several tasks.

items.text: (i) We release SCIBERT, a new resource demonstrated to improve performance on a range of NLP tasks in the scientiﬁc domain.
items.plain: We present SCIBERT, a resource that improves language processing task performance in science.

items.text: Corpus We train SCIBERT on a random sample of 1.14M papers from Semantic Scholar (Ammar et al., 2018).
items.why: Describes the training dataset size and source.
items.plain: We train SCIBERT on 1.14M randomly selected papers from Semantic Scholar.

items.text: We observe that SCIBERT outperforms BERT-Base on scientiﬁc tasks (+2.11 F1 with ﬁnetuning and +2.43 F1 without)8.
items.why: Gives the headline quantitative improvement on scientific tasks.
items.plain: SCIBERT beats BERT-Base on scientific tasks, gaining +2.11 F1 with fine-tuning and +2.43 F1 without.

items.text: We observe that SCIBERT outperforms BERT- Base on biomedical tasks (+1.92 F1 with ﬁnetuning and +3.59 F1 without).
items.why: Gives the core improvement score on biomedical tasks.
items.plain: SCIBERT beats BERT-Base on biomedical tasks by +1.92 F1 with fine-tuning and +3.59 F1 without.

items.text: We observe that SCIBERT outperforms BERT- Base on computer science tasks (+3.55 F1 with ﬁnetuning and +1.13 F1 without).
items.why: Gives the core improvement score on computer science tasks.
items.plain: SCIBERT beats BERT-Base on computer science tasks by +3.55 F1 with fine-tuning and +1.13 F1 without.

items.text: We observe improved results via BERT ﬁnetuning rather than task-speciﬁc architectures atop frozen embeddings (+3.25 F1 with SCIBERT and +3.58 with BERT-Base, on average).
items.why: States takeaway about fine-tuning versus fixed embeddings.
items.plain: Fine-tuning BERT works better than putting task architectures on top of frozen embeddings.

items.text: Given the disjoint vocabularies (Section 2) and the magnitude of improvement over BERT-Base (Section 4), we suspect that while an in-domain vocabulary is helpful, SCIBERT beneﬁts most from the scientiﬁc corpus pretraining.
items.why: Delivers the core takeaway explaining why SCIBERT works.
items.plain: An in-domain vocabulary helps, but SCIBERT gets most of its benefit from pretraining on the scientific text corpus.
